items.followUp: Describe three uses of radioisotopes in the treatment or diagnosis of diseases.

rubric.why: Identifies a radiotherapy isotope and its use against cancer.
rubric.description: Cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy to treat cancer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for cobalt-60 and 1 mark for its use in cancer treatment; accept equivalent wording about its gamma rays destroying cancer cells.

rubric.why: Names an isotope used for thyroid disorders.
rubric.description: Iodine-131 is used to diagnose or treat thyroid disorders.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking iodine-131 with the thyroid.

rubric.why: Gives a medical tracer application.
rubric.description: Sodium-24 can be used as a tracer to study blood circulation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking sodium-24 with tracing blood circulation.

rubric.why: Gives a further medical treatment application.
rubric.description: Phosphorus-32 is used in the treatment of some blood diseases, including leukemia.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking phosphorus-32 with leukemia or a blood disease.

modelAnswer: Cobalt-60 emits gamma rays that are used in radiotherapy to destroy cancer cells.
Iodine-131 is used to diagnose or treat disorders of the thyroid gland.
Sodium-24 is used as a radioactive tracer to study blood circulation.
Phosphorus-32 is used in the treatment of some blood diseases, including leukemia.

items.followUp: Define proton number and neutron number, and find both for a sodium-23 atom.

rubric.why: Atomic number is defined by the number of protons in the nucleus.
rubric.description: Defines atomic number as the number of protons in an atom's nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: A correct example demonstrates the atomic-number definition.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example, such as carbon having atomic number 6.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct element and atomic number.

rubric.why: Mass number counts both protons and neutrons.
rubric.description: Defines mass number as the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: A correct example demonstrates the mass-number definition.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example, such as carbon-12, with mass number 12.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example; accept carbon-12 or another correctly specified nuclide.

modelAnswer: Atomic number (Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
For example, carbon has atomic number 6.
Mass number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
For example, carbon-12 has mass number 12 (6 protons and 6 neutrons).

items.followUp: Explain how a single covalent bond differs from a double covalent bond, giving an example of each.

rubric.why: A covalent bond is formed by sharing electron pairs between atoms.
rubric.description: Defines a covalent bond as a bond formed when atoms share electron pairs.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a clear definition; award 1 mark if sharing is mentioned but the definition is incomplete.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond involves one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.description: Explains the single covalent bond and gives H₂ as an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct description and example.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond involves two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.description: Explains the double covalent bond and gives O₂ as an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct description and example.

rubric.why: A triple covalent bond involves three shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.description: Explains the triple covalent bond and gives N₂ as an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct description and example.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond has one shared pair of electrons; an example is H₂.
A double covalent bond has two shared pairs of electrons; an example is O₂.
A triple covalent bond has three shared pairs of electrons; an example is N₂.

items.followUp: Define a heterogeneous mixture and give one example.

rubric.why: A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout.
rubric.description: Defines a homogeneous mixture as having uniform composition throughout.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining feature.

rubric.why: A suitable example applies the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example, such as salt water or air.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout.
Salt water is an example of a homogeneous mixture.

items.followUp: State what the atomic number and mass number tell us about an atom.

rubric.why: Atomic number counts the protons in an atom's nucleus.
rubric.description: States that atomic number is the number of protons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct meaning of atomic number.

rubric.why: Mass number is the total of the protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct meaning of mass number.

modelAnswer: Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in its nucleus.

items.followUp: What are isotopes? Give two isotopes of hydrogen as an example.

rubric.why: Isotopes have the same proton number but different mass numbers.
rubric.description: Defines isotopes by their same atomic number and different mass numbers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both parts of the definition.

rubric.why: A valid pair illustrates the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as hydrogen-1 and hydrogen-2.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct isotope example.

modelAnswer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
Hydrogen-1 and hydrogen-2 are examples of isotopes.

items.followUp: Describe cathode rays and name the scientist who discovered them.

rubric.why: Cathode rays are streams of electrons emitted from the cathode.
rubric.description: Identifies cathode rays as streams of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing cathode rays.

rubric.why: J. J. Thomson discovered cathode rays.
rubric.description: Names J. J. Thomson as the discoverer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct scientist.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays are streams of electrons emitted from the cathode in a discharge tube.
They were discovered by J. J. Thomson.

items.followUp: Why are Group 18 elements called noble gases? Give one example.

rubric.why: Noble gases are very unreactive because their outer electron shells are complete.
rubric.description: Explains that noble gases are chemically inert or have complete outer shells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation.

rubric.why: A Group 18 element is a valid example.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as helium or neon.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct noble gas.

modelAnswer: Noble gases are Group 18 elements; they are very unreactive because their outer electron shells are complete.
Helium is an example of a noble gas.
